title: Verifier‑Assisted versus LLM‑Only Pre‑deployment Network‑Change Validation: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We evaluate whether adding a deterministic pre‑deployment verifier plus a bounded automated repair budget increases the fraction of intent‑driven network‑change proposals that pass semantic validation compared with accepting a single LLM candidate. In a preregistered paired design (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) we executed 300 paired intents (100 per difficulty stratum: low/medium/high) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic semantic validator. Each pair reused the same single LLM generation (shared_initial) for two conditions: baseline (accept single shot) and guarded (validator + ≤1 automated repair). Results: baseline 299/300 unflagged verifier passes (0.9966667), guarded 300/300 (1.0); contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.01] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, B = 10000). Under the supplied synthetic suite and the constrained repair operator the single‑shot generator was near ceiling, limiting observable deterministic rescue to a single sequencing omission corrected by one automated edit. We archive the preregistration, execution, validator traces, and analysis artifacts and interpret the findings with respect to estimand conditioning, validator coverage, repair budget, and operational policy.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are being applied to network operations (NetOps) tasks including intent→configuration translation, template synthesis, and automated repair. For pre‑deployment network changes, semantic correctness is operationally critical: sequencing constraints, reachability, and policy preservation must hold before changes are committed. A common engineering pattern couples a generative model with deterministic validators and bounded automated repair (generate→validate→repair) to reduce operational risk. However, the measurable benefit of such guarded pipelines depends on the estimand (what is held fixed), the generator's single‑shot quality, the validator's expressiveness, and the permitted repair budget. Prior evaluations often conflate verifier benefit with benefits arising from resampling or verifier‑guided regeneration, making the isolated effect of deterministic validator+repair unclear.

Motivated by operational policies that limit model calls for cost, latency, or governance reasons, we preregistered a paired experiment to isolate the deterministic rescue attributable to a verifier and a bounded repair operator when the same single LLM candidate is reused across conditions. The primary research question: does adding a deterministic verifier plus at most one automated repair increase the probability that a single LLM candidate passes semantic pre‑deployment validation compared with accepting that same candidate without repair? Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired evaluation using a shared_initial estimand that conditions on one LLM draw per intent; (2) a complete archived execution and analysis bundle including validator traces and the single automated repair transcript; and (3) an evidence‑grounded interpretation that links estimator conditioning, ceiling effects, and operational implications for NetOps CI/CD policies.
sections.related_work:
Recent surveys and system papers document rapid adoption of LLMs for NetOps tasks and articulate architectures that combine LLMs with external tools and validators [1–4]. Tool‑augmented frameworks (planner‑centric, ReAct‑style) enable LLMs to call deterministic checkers or simulators to decompose multi‑step workflows and coordinate corrective actions [2]. Empirical reports indicate that generate→validate→repair scaffolds can improve correctness metrics over unconstrained generation, but gains depend strongly on validator coverage, task distribution, and whether pipelines permit resampling or interactive steering [3–5]. Work on hallucination detection and deterministic safety nets proposes entropy‑based detectors, retrieval augmentation, and constrained edit operators to reduce semantic errors [6]. Studies combining symbolic fault localization with generative repair show promise but vary by fault class and verifier expressiveness [5,7,8].

Two methodological concerns from this literature informed our design. First, evaluations that allow multiple independent model draws conflate deterministic verifier effects with resampling benefits; to bound the pure post‑hoc rescue effect we reuse a single candidate across conditions. Second, many public NetOps benchmarks emphasize syntactic correctness rather than semantically rich invariants (reachability, sequencing, policy preservation); our synthetic suite encodes sequencing and reachability invariants to better reflect pre‑deployment checks.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. We preregistered the confirmatory paired design (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) and fixed the primary estimand: the absolute paired difference in unflagged verifier‑pass proportion (guarded − baseline) on N = 300 paired intents after prespecified inclusion/exclusion rules. The confirmatory executor and inferential procedures (exact two‑sided McNemar and paired bootstrap percentile CI) were fixed prior to the main run; exploratory subgroup tests were labeled and multiplicity plans specified.

Task suite and stratification. Tasks were generated deterministically into a synthetic topology suite and stratified into low/medium/high difficulty by measurable metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, required_command_count). The confirmatory main run sampled 100 paired intents per stratum to ensure balanced difficulty coverage. Each task manifest encodes the natural‑language intent, initial and expected final device states, sequencing constraints (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields), protected interfaces, and required command sequences; these semantic invariants are the basis of deterministic validation.

Shared_initial protocol and model configuration. To isolate deterministic verifier/repair effects from resampling, each pair used a single shared_initial generation drawn from the declared generator (gpt-5-mini) which was evaluated under both conditions. The guarded condition applies a deterministic validator and permits at most one automated, constrained edit if the validator flags the candidate. The baseline condition accepts the shared_initial candidate without repair. This shared_initial estimand corresponds to operational policies that budget a single generation per change request.

Validator and repair operator. Semantic evaluation used a deterministic, rule‑based validator that checks sequencing invariants, required command counts, preservation of unspecified state, topology reachability invariants encoded by the suite, and forbidden‑template protections for protected interfaces. Scoring is binary: an unflagged candidate passes. The repair operator is a constrained edit routine limited to localized insertions or ordering edits (e.g., inserting a missing "admin down" before a VLAN/MTU change). Repair is applied deterministically and re‑validated; if flags persist the guarded attempt counts as a failure.

Execution, contamination controls, and missingness rules. The confirmatory execution enforced the preregistered stopping rule and exclusion logic: pairs excluded only if both pipeline calls failed due to provider/infrastructure outages. Negative controls and deterministic contamination checks were included per stratum. All provider events, stage counts, and validator traces were recorded and archived for auditability. Analysis followed the preregistered paired executor with exact two‑sided McNemar inference and a paired bootstrap (seed = 1729, B = 10000) to obtain a 95% percentile CI for the paired difference.
sections.results:
Execution summary and accounting. The confirmatory run completed 600 episodes (300 pairs) under the shared_initial protocol with a single declared generator model. The empirical model‑call footprint was low: one shared_initial generation per pair and a single repair invocation across all pairs.

Primary outcomes. Binary scoring yielded baseline_success_count = 299 and guarded_success_count = 300 (baseline rate = 299/300 = 0.9966667; guarded rate = 300/300 = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar test on the discordant counts (n10 and n01) returned p = 1.0. The absolute paired difference (guarded − baseline) equals 0.0033333. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (seed = 1729, B = 10000) is [0.00, 0.01]. Because discordance is minimal (m = 1) the exact test lacks power to detect small differences; the bootstrap CI bounds the plausible absolute improvement to at most one percentage point under the studied estimand and suite.

Per‑stratum diagnostics and repair trace. Stratum tallies: low baseline = 100/100, guarded = 100/100; medium baseline = 100/100, guarded = 100/100; high baseline = 99/100, guarded = 100/100. The solitary discordant episode occurred in the high stratum and invoked the permitted automated repair. Validator traces attribute the initial failure to a sequencing omission: the shared_initial candidate lacked an explicit 'admin down' before a VLAN/MTU change required by intent. The constrained repair performed one local insertion, after which the validator reported the corrected candidate as valid. This single deterministic rescue required one additional repair invocation across 300 pairs, indicating negligible extra model‑call cost under the chosen design.

Contamination and missingness. Preplanned contamination checks and negative controls signaled no unexpected contaminations; no pairs were excluded under preregistered rules. All episodes were scorable under the deterministic validator's parsing rules.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation with respect to estimand conditioning. The shared_initial estimand measures only deterministic validator and bounded repair rescue applied to an identical LLM candidate. It therefore excludes verifier benefits that arise from resampling, verifier‑guided regeneration, or interactive steering; those alternate estimands are relevant for operational policies that allow additional model calls. Under policies that strictly limit model calls per change, our design provides an operationally meaningful bound on deterministic rescue.

Ceiling effects and pilot omission. Baseline single‑shot performance was near ceiling (299/300) on the chosen synthetic suite, producing minimal discordance (m = 1) and correspondingly limited inferential sensitivity for small absolute improvements. The preregistration included an optional small pilot for discordance estimation and power calibration; that pilot was not executed and therefore the main run faced reduced ability to detect modest effects. In practice, small calibration pilots can inform sample sizing when generator performance may approach ceiling on targeted task suites.

Validator coverage and failure‑mode dependence. The single observed failure mode was a sequencing omission; more complex failure classes (reachability violations, ACL semantics violations) were not prevalent in this synthetic distribution. The guarded pipeline's marginal utility will increase for task populations where validator‑detectable failure modes are more common or where validators check richer semantics. Conversely, if operator policy forbids automated edits, the guarded pipeline's operational value reduces to detection and escalation rather than automated rescue.

Repair budget tradeoffs and operational cost. We intentionally constrained repair to a single localized edit to quantify bounded deterministic rescue; iterative or more expressive repair operators would likely increase rescue rates but change the estimand and impose additional model‑call cost. Empirically, a single permitted repair produced one rescue with one extra invocation across 300 pairs, demonstrating low marginal model‑call overhead in this run. Organizations should weigh repair budgets, estimand choice, and model‑call cost when designing deployment policies.

Implications for NetOps evaluation practice. Evaluations should align estimands with deployment policies: if resampling is permitted operationally, experiments must allow independent additional model draws to measure achievable success under that policy. When model calls are constrained, the shared_initial estimand provides a conservative operationally relevant bound for deterministic rescue. Finally, benchmark suites should encode semantically rich invariants (sequencing, reachability, policy preservation) to surface operationally meaningful failures rather than only syntactic errors.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired study conditioning on a single LLM draw per intent, a deterministic validator plus a bounded automated repair budget produced one deterministic rescue out of 300 pairs when compared with accepting the same single candidate without repair. Baseline single‑shot generation was near ceiling (299/300), yielding an absolute paired improvement of 0.00333 (exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.01]). Under operational policies that limit model calls, the guarded generate→validate→repair pattern can produce deterministic rescues at low marginal model‑call cost, but the observable benefit depends strongly on task distribution, validator expressiveness, and permitted repair operators. We release the preregistration, execution traces, validator diagnostics, and analysis artifacts to enable targeted follow‑up studies that vary estimand conditioning, model strength, task heterogeneity, and repair budgets.

limitations: Synthetic benchmark: tasks and topologies were generated deterministically; real‑world heterogeneity may reveal different failure modes and increase the marginal utility of guarded pipelines.
Single model and validator: only gpt-5-mini and the declared deterministic validator were evaluated; generalization to other LLMs or richer validators is not demonstrated.
Ceiling effect: baseline single‑shot performance approached 100% on the chosen suite (299/300), reducing observable discordance and limiting statistical sensitivity to small absolute improvements.
Pilot not executed: the preregistered optional pilot for discordance estimation/power calibration was not run, so the main sample size faced unanticipated ceiling performance.

Estimand conditioning: the shared_initial protocol conditions on a single LLM draw and therefore does not measure verifier benefits that arise from resampling, verifier‑guided regeneration, or interactive steering.
Repair budget: the guarded condition permitted at most one constrained automated edit; iterative or more expressive repair strategies may yield different outcomes and were not tested here.
